doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

chapter: Studio craft and the TV and rock dates
title: Sight-reading and the disco period
summary: Shew describes how he handled sixteenth-note-heavy disco charts and calls the music percussive and unmelodic.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well when you went in, you’d go in and you’d sit down in the chair and someone would pass out the music. Did you have a routine — let me start again — I try to tell my students when they get a piece of music, you know normally what younger people do is they get a piece of music and they immediately start going [scats] they look at one measure and they try to play it or something. And I’m wondering what did you guys do to give yourself the best chance to play it and not become a two-take player.

Well I guess everybody has their own approach to that. A lot of it has to do with your attitude with you, if you feel confident in your sight reading skills, which I was always very good at, you know, I never had to worry, I could pretty much sight read. The only things I ever had any real complicated times with sight reading were during the disco period, when everything was all sixteenth notes [scats] damn it, how many sixteenth rests are there in this measure you know? And you’d have to sit there and visually like uhh — you know you get the point. Those were difficult. But there’s a way to solve it, you make an imaginary line, if it’s a 4/4 bar, down the middle of the bar and you start isolating where the one and the two and the three and the four are in the beat, in the measure. And once you see that then you can place those rest kind of things — because they were writing everything like instead of eighth notes, sixteenths and stuff like that a lot. And someone would start writing a sixteenth note and then two sixteenth rests and then another sixteenth. Holy crap that’s only two beats you know? Or it’s one beat. Or wait a minute, how many is that?
It almost sounds like — it sounds like they were trying to orchestrate what a guitar does, a rhythm guitar, like [scats].

And the drums, and the percussion. It’s like all of that music was mostly percussive music. It’s not very melodic. It’s all rhythmic for the most part you know. And I don’t remember any disco tune that had a melody I wanted to sing back — you know come home and sing this to my wife, oh wait ‘til you hear this disco song I recorded today. It was like [scats percussively].

Well you just anticipated a question I have right in front of me. You can’t see it, but the question was what kind of thing would happen on a studio date that you would come home and it was interesting enough to tell your wife about?
